source.name: VocabBuilder starter set (Southern Vietnamese)
source.notes: Hand-written by an AI assistant (Claude) as a small starter set for VocabBuilder. Not corpus-derived: curatedOrder is a teaching order, not a frequency rank. Review and edit freely.

senses.note: Used for both hello and goodbye, normally followed by a kinship pronoun: Chào anh, Chào chị, Chào em.

examples.text: Tui về nha, chào mọi người!

grammar.notes: Xin chào is a polite, rather formal 'hello' (textbooks, announcements); in everyday Saigon speech people say chào + pronoun.
Grammatically a verb ('to thank'): add the person you're thanking: Cám ơn chị (thank you, to a woman a bit older).

entries.regionalNote: Cám ơn reflects the Southern pronunciation and is a common, accepted spelling; cảm ơn is the standard spelling used nationwide (and the Northern pronunciation).

senses.note: Also 'excuse me' to get someone's attention politely.

examples.text: Xin lỗi anh, cho em hỏi chút.
examples.translation: Excuse me, can I ask you something?

grammar.notes: Grammatically a verb ('to apologize'): Em xin lỗi chị (I apologize to you).

entries.regionalNote: Trễ (late) in the first example is the Southern word; Northern: muộn.

senses.note: Polite yes or response word when speaking to someone older or of higher status; also put before an answer to sound respectful.

examples.text: Dạ, chị chờ em xíu nha.

grammar.notes: Casual 'yeah' between friends: ừ. Also the polite answer when someone calls you: —Lan ơi! —Dạ!

entries.regionalNote: Dạ is the everyday polite 'yes' in the South; Northern speakers more often say vâng. Xíu (a little bit) in the example is Southern colloquial.

senses.note: Before a verb or adjective it means 'not': Tui không biết (I don't know).

grammar.notes: At the end of a sentence it turns it into a yes/no question: Anh khỏe không? (Are you well?). Answer with có or dạ (yes) or không (no).

entries.regionalNote: In casual Southern speech it often sounds like hông: Biết hông? (You know?)

senses.note: For someone younger than you (e.g. a waiter or shop assistant). The younger person also calls themselves em (= I/me).

examples.text: Em ơi, cho anh một ly trà đá.
examples.translation: Excuse me, a glass of iced tea, please.

examples.text: Em là sinh viên năm hai.
Em gái tui mới vào đại học.
examples.translation: My younger sister just started university.

grammar.notes: Vietnamese uses kinship words as pronouns, chosen by relative age. Add ơi to call someone: Em ơi! (Excuse me!, to a younger server).

senses.note: For a man a bit older than you, or a man of about your age you don't know well. He also calls himself anh (= I/me).

examples.text: Anh ơi, cho em hỏi đường.
examples.translation: Excuse me, could you tell me the way?

examples.text: Anh trai tui làm ở Sài Gòn.
examples.translation: My older brother works in Saigon.

grammar.notes: anh trai = older brother; anh ấy = he/him (a young man), in casual Southern speech often contracted to ảnh.

senses.note: For a woman a bit older than you, or a woman of about your age you don't know well. She also calls herself chị (= I/me).

examples.text: Chị ơi, tính tiền giùm em.
examples.translation: Excuse me, can I have the bill, please?

examples.text: Chị tui có hai đứa con.
examples.translation: My older sister has two kids.

grammar.notes: chị gái = older sister; chị ấy = she/her (a young woman), in casual Southern speech often contracted to chỉ.

entries.regionalNote: Giùm (for me, on my behalf) in the example is Southern; Northern: giúp or hộ.

senses.note: Casual, friendly 'I/me', mostly between people of about the same age.

grammar.notes: Plural: tụi tui or tụi mình (we, casual). With older people use a kinship word instead (em, con).

entries.regionalNote: Southern colloquial form of tôi. Tôi is neutral to formal everywhere and can sound distant in casual Saigon conversation.

senses.note: Links two nouns: Tui là giáo viên (I'm a teacher).

grammar.notes: Not used before adjectives: Tui mệt (I'm tired), not tui là mệt.

senses.note: Also 'yes' in answer to có…không? questions: Anh có xe không? — Có.

examples.text: Em có anh chị em không?

grammar.notes: có + verb + không? asks 'do/does…?': Anh có hút thuốc không? (Do you smoke?)

examples.translation: I want to go to Đà Lạt.

examples.text: Em muốn ăn phở hay hủ tiếu?
examples.translation: Do you want phở or hủ tiếu?

grammar.notes: hay = 'or' in questions.

entries.regionalNote: Hủ tiếu (in the example) is the classic Southern noodle soup.

senses.note: Also 'to travel by': đi xe buýt (go by bus).

examples.translation: Tomorrow I'm going to Vũng Tàu.

grammar.notes: At the end of a sentence đi means 'go ahead / let's': Ăn đi! (Eat up!), Mình đi ăn đi! (Let's go eat!)
…chưa? asks '…yet?': Ăn chưa? (Have you eaten yet?). Answer rồi (yes, already) or chưa (not yet).

examples.translation: What would you like to drink?

examples.text: Trời nóng quá, uống nước đi!
examples.translation: It's so hot, drink some water!

senses.note: Also any drink: nước cam (orange juice), nước mía (sugarcane juice).

examples.translation: Could I have a glass of water?

examples.text: Cho em một ly cà phê sữa đá.
examples.translation: One iced coffee with milk, please.

examples.text: Sáng nào tui cũng uống cà phê.

entries.regionalNote: Saigon's classic is cà phê sữa đá; in the North the same drink is usually called nâu đá.

senses.note: Also a measure word for drinks: một ly cà phê (a cup of coffee).

examples.text: Cho em hai ly trà đá.
examples.translation: Two glasses of iced tea, please.

examples.text: Uống thêm một ly nữa đi!

entries.regionalNote: Southern; Northern: cốc.

grammar.notes: For small numbers people often use mấy instead: Mấy giờ rồi? (What time is it?), Mấy người? (How many people?)

entries.regionalNote: In fast Southern speech often shortened to nhiêu: Nhiêu tiền? (How much?)

expressions.translation: to get the bill; to pay

senses.note: General classifier for objects, placed before the noun: một cái ly (a glass). Cái này = this one; cái kia = that one.

examples.text: Cái này ngon lắm, ăn thử đi!
examples.translation: This one is really good, try it!

grammar.notes: Classifiers go between a number and a noun: hai cái ly (two glasses). Animals use con: con heo (a pig).

examples.translation: What do you want to eat?

grammar.notes: Question words stay where the answer would go, usually at the end: Anh ăn gì? (lit. 'You eat what?')

examples.translation: Where shall we go for lunch?

grammar.notes: Goes at the end: Anh đi đâu? (Where are you going?), … ở đâu? (Where is …?)

entries.regionalNote: Vậy at the end of a question (Northern: thế) is very common in the South: Anh đi đâu vậy?

senses.note: Sentence-final particle that softens requests, suggestions and promises and makes them friendly.

examples.translation: Wait for me a sec, OK?

entries.regionalNote: Southern; Northern: nhé.

examples.text: Anh nói tiếng Việt giỏi quá!
Chị nói chậm lại giùm em nha.
examples.translation: Could you speak more slowly, please?

entries.regionalNote: In requests Southerners add giùm ('for me'); Northern: giúp or hộ.

senses.note: biết + verb = know how to / can: Em biết bơi không? (Can you swim?)

examples.text: Anh biết nói tiếng Anh không?

senses.note: Khỏe không? = How are you? (lit. 'Are you well?')

grammar.notes: Also spelled khoẻ (newer tone-mark placement); both are correct.

examples.translation: The food at this place is really good.

examples.text: Mắc quá, bớt chút đi chị!
examples.translation: Too expensive, can you knock a bit off?

examples.text: Đồ ăn ở đây hơi mắc.
examples.translation: The food here is a bit pricey.

grammar.notes: bớt = to lower the price (when bargaining).

entries.regionalNote: Southern; Northern: đắt.

examples.text: Đồ ở chợ rẻ hơn siêu thị.
examples.translation: Things at the market are cheaper than at the supermarket.

grammar.notes: Comparisons use hơn: rẻ hơn (cheaper), mắc hơn (more expensive).

senses.note: Cooked rice, and by extension a meal: ăn cơm = to have a meal. Uncooked rice is gạo.

examples.text: Trưa nay mình ăn cơm tấm nha.
examples.translation: Let's have broken rice for lunch today.

expressions.translation: broken rice, a Saigon classic usually served with grilled pork

senses.note: Both the airy baguette-style bread and the famous filled sandwich.

examples.text: Sáng nay tui ăn bánh mì.
examples.translation: I had a bánh mì this morning.

examples.text: Cho em một ổ bánh mì thịt.
examples.translation: One bánh mì with cold cuts, please.

grammar.notes: Classifier in the South: ổ (một ổ bánh mì = one loaf / one sandwich).

entries.regionalNote: Northern speakers usually say một chiếc or một cái bánh mì.

grammar.notes: tên can work like a verb: Em tên Lan (My name's Lan). In Vietnamese names the given name comes last, and that's the name people use.

examples.text: Chị là người Sài Gòn hả?

grammar.notes: người + place = someone from there: người Việt (Vietnamese person), người Mỹ (American). Also the classifier for people: hai người (two people).

senses.note: Neutral 'you' between people of similar age, and in ads and apps.

grammar.notes: bạn bè = friends (collectively); bạn trai / bạn gái = boyfriend / girlfriend.

examples.text: Ba tui làm tài xế taxi.
examples.translation: My dad is a taxi driver.

examples.text: Ba ơi, con đi học nha!
examples.translation: Bye, Dad, I'm off to school!

grammar.notes: Also used as a pronoun: children call their father ba and themselves con. Ba is also the number three.

entries.regionalNote: Southern; Northern: bố.

examples.translation: Mom is a really good cook.
I miss you so much, Mom!

grammar.notes: Used as a pronoun like ba: Con nhớ má (I miss you, Mom). Má also means 'cheek'.

entries.regionalNote: Traditional Southern word; Northern: mẹ. Many people in Saigon today also say mẹ (ba mẹ = parents).

examples.text: Cho em hỏi nhà vệ sinh ở đâu?
Nhà vệ sinh ở trên lầu.

entries.regionalNote: Lầu (floor, upstairs) in the example is Southern; Northern: tầng or gác.

senses.note: Anh ở đâu? = Where do you live? / Where are you?
As a preposition: ở nhà (at home), ở Sài Gòn (in Saigon).

examples.text: Tui ở gần chợ Bến Thành.
examples.translation: I live near Bến Thành Market.

senses.note: To go back to where you belong: về nhà (go home), về quê (go back to one's hometown).

examples.translation: What time will you be home?
This Tết I'm going back to my hometown.

grammar.notes: Also the preposition 'about': nói về (talk about).
Also 'in/into' after another verb: bỏ vô (put in).

entries.regionalNote: Southern; Northern and formal written Vietnamese: vào. Nè (in the example) is a Southern particle for drawing attention (Northern: này).

senses.note: làm or làm việc = to work: Em làm ở đâu? (Where do you work?)

examples.translation: What do you do for a living?

examples.text: Hôm nay tui phải làm tới tối.
examples.translation: Today I have to work until evening.
I want to buy this one.

examples.text: Chị mua trái cây ở đâu vậy?
examples.translation: Where did you buy the fruit?

senses.note: Often shortened to giờ in speech: Giờ mình đi đâu? (Where to now?)

examples.text: Bây giờ tui bận, lát gọi lại nha.
examples.translation: I'm busy right now, I'll call you back in a bit.

examples.text: Hôm nay trời mưa lớn quá.

entries.regionalNote: In casual Southern speech you'll also hear bữa nay.

senses.note: Often just mai: Mai gặp nha! (See you tomorrow!)

examples.text: Ngày mai em có rảnh không?
Ngày mai tui đi làm sớm.
examples.translation: I'm going to work early tomorrow.

senses.note: After a verb: done, already: Em ăn rồi (I've already eaten). The opposite is chưa (not yet).
Linking actions: Ăn xong rồi đi (Finish eating, then go).

examples.text: Mình ăn cơm rồi đi cà phê nha.
examples.translation: Let's eat and then go for coffee.

senses.note: After an adjective it means 'so' or 'too', depending on context: Ngon quá! (So good!), Nhanh quá (Too fast).

examples.text: Em nói nhanh quá, anh không hiểu.
examples.translation: You're speaking too fast, I can't follow.

entries.regionalNote: Common Southern colloquial intensifiers: quá trời (Nóng quá trời! = So hot!) and ghê (Đẹp ghê! = So pretty!).

examples.text: Mình gặp nhau lúc bảy giờ nha.

grammar.notes: Clock time: bảy giờ (7 o'clock), bảy giờ rưỡi (7:30). Mấy giờ? = What time?

examples.text: Điện thoại em hết pin rồi.
Cho tui xin số điện thoại nha.
examples.translation: Can I get your phone number?

senses.note: In everyday talk often just xe. A motorbike taxi is xe ôm.

examples.text: Tui đi làm bằng xe máy.
examples.translation: I go to work by motorbike.

examples.text: Xe máy của anh để ở đâu?
examples.translation: Where did you park your motorbike?
The traffic on this road is terrible!

examples.text: Cà phê ít đường nha em.

grammar.notes: Street names: đường Lê Lợi (Lê Lợi Street).

entries.regionalNote: Traffic jam: kẹt xe in the South, tắc đường in the North.

examples.text: Má đi chợ từ sáng sớm.
examples.translation: Mom went to the market early this morning.
Bến Thành Market is really crowded.

expressions.translation: to go (food) shopping at the market

examples.text: Tui thích ăn trái cây lắm.
Chợ này bán trái cây rẻ.

grammar.notes: Before a fruit's name Southerners use trái: trái xoài (mango), trái dừa (coconut).

entries.regionalNote: Southern; Northern: hoa quả (and quả instead of trái: quả xoài).

senses.note: With food it means pork: thịt heo (pork), sườn heo (pork ribs).

grammar.notes: Animals take the classifier con: con heo (a pig).

entries.regionalNote: Southern; Northern: lợn (thịt lợn). Mập (fat) in the example is also Southern; Northern: béo.

grammar.notes: Also 'grown-up': người lớn (adult).

entries.regionalNote: In the South lớn (or casual bự) is the everyday word; Northern speakers often say to.

examples.text: Cho chị một ly nhỏ thôi.
examples.translation: Just a small one for me, please.

examples.text: Hồi nhỏ tui ở Cần Thơ.
examples.translation: When I was little, I lived in Cần Thơ.

entries.regionalNote: In the South nhỏ is the everyday word; Northern speakers often say bé.

examples.text: Cẩn thận, tô phở còn nóng.
examples.translation: Careful, the phở is still hot.

entries.regionalNote: Tô (a big noodle bowl) is Southern; Northern: bát. Quá trời (so very) is Southern colloquial.

examples.text: Cái áo dài này đẹp ghê!

entries.regionalNote: Ghê (so, really) after an adjective is Southern colloquial.
